blocks.content: A resource request declares what a container actually needs to run properly, and this is not just documentation, it is the exact number the scheduler uses to decide which node a Pod can actually fit on.

A request specifies the CPU and memory a container needs under normal operation, this is meant to be a realistic figure, not padded or guessed at randomly, since it directly drives real scheduling decisions.

blocks.alt: A realistic figure, not a guess, since it drives real decisions

blocks.content: This is the practical payoff, exactly as covered in the Scheduler topic in the Architecture module, the scheduler considers a Pod's resource requests when deciding which node has enough genuinely free capacity to actually run it.

blocks.alt: The exact number the scheduler weighs when picking a node

blocks.content: 3. A Node's Capacity Must Cover It
blocks.text: 3. A Node's Capacity Must Cover It

blocks.content: Concretely, the scheduler will not place a Pod on a node unless that node has at least as much unallocated capacity as the Pod's requests declare, this is a hard constraint on placement, not a soft suggestion.

blocks.alt: A hard placement constraint, not advisory guidance

blocks.content: 4. A Guaranteed Minimum, Not a Cap
blocks.text: 4. A Guaranteed Minimum, Not a Cap

blocks.content: It is worth being precise here: a request is a guaranteed floor, the container is assured at least this much, it says nothing about the maximum it is allowed to use, that is a completely separate concept, Resource Limits, covered in the very next topic.

blocks.alt: A floor, not a ceiling, the ceiling is a different, separate setting

blocks.content: 5. Seeing It in a Real Manifest
blocks.text: 5. Seeing It in a Real Manifest

blocks.content: A typical, modest web application might declare something like a quarter of a CPU core and 256MB of memory as its baseline requirement, real values, sized to what the application genuinely needs to function normally.

blocks.alt: Real, sized values, not arbitrary placeholders

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: Resource requests declare what a container genuinely needs, and the scheduler uses this exact number to decide which node has enough free capacity to place it on.
A request is a guaranteed minimum, not a maximum, the corresponding ceiling is a separate concept, Resource Limits, covered next.
